Coherent Without Grounding, Grounded Without Success: Observability and Epistemic Failure

Camilo Chacón Sartori Email: camilo.chacon@icn2.cat; cchacon@iiia.csic.es Affiliation: Institut Català de Nanociència i Nanotecnologia (ICN2) Affiliation: Artificial Intelligence Research Institute (IIIA-CSIC), Barcelona, Spain
Abstract

When an agent can articulate why something works, we typically take this as evidence of genuine understanding. This presupposes that effective action and correct explanation covary, and that coherent explanation reliably signals both. I argue that this assumption fails for contemporary Large Language Models (LLMs). I introduce what I call the Bidirectional Coherence Paradox: competence and grounding not only dissociate but invert across epistemic conditions. In low-observability domains, LLMs often act successfully while misidentifying the mechanisms that produce their success. In high-observability domains, they frequently generate explanations that accurately track observable causal structure yet fail to translate those diagnoses into effective intervention. In both cases, explanatory coherence remains intact, obscuring the underlying dissociation. Drawing on experiments in compiler optimization and hyperparameter tuning, I develop the Epistemic Triangle, a model of how priors, signals, and domain knowledge interact under varying observability. The results suggest that neither behavioral success nor explanatory accuracy alone suffices for attributing understanding. I argue that evaluating artificial epistemic agents requires a tripartite framework—coherence, grounding, and a proper basing relation linking explanation to action. The systematic separation of knowing-that and knowing-how in LLMs thus challenges assumptions inherited from both epistemology and current AI evaluation practice.

keywords
Epistemology, Artificial Intelligence, Coherence Paradox, Large Language Models, Grounding, Pragmatic Competence, Knowing-that/Knowing-how, Abductive Reasoning, Epistemic Luck, Confabulation

1 Introduction

The poet is a faker / Who’s so good at his act / He even fakes the pain / Of pain he feels in fact.

Fernando Pessoa, Autopsychography (trans. Richard Zenith)

1.1 The Epistemological Challenge of AI Explanation

The capacity to generate fluent explanations has long been considered a sign of understanding. When a human expert explains why a particular solution works, this is typically taken as evidence that they grasp the underlying causal structure of the domain. But what happens when the explanation comes from an artificial system whose relationship to its own outputs remains fundamentally opaque?

Large Language Models (LLMs) now routinely generate explanations exhibiting the hallmarks of genuine understanding: logical coherence, domain-appropriate terminology, and confident articulation of causal mechanisms. Yet whether these outputs reflect processes genuinely analogous to comprehension or merely sophisticated pattern completion remains a deeply nuanced question. Recent work suggests that LLM architectures produce patterns of error in code generation that diverge systematically from those observed in humans (Chacón Sartori, 2026), raising broader questions about whether coherent outputs reliably signal genuine competence.

The stakes of this question extend beyond academic philosophy. As LLMs become integrated into high-stakes decision-making—medical diagnosis, legal reasoning, scientific research—the assumption that explanatory fluency signals epistemic reliability becomes practically consequential. If systems can produce compelling explanations without exhibiting the functional properties we associate with genuine competence, then the very features we use to assess trustworthiness may systematically mislead us.

1.2 Situating the Problem

The concern that artificial systems might “explain without understanding” connects to several longstanding debates in philosophy of mind and epistemology:

The Symbol Grounding Problem. Harnad (1990) argued that symbolic AI systems manipulate meaningless tokens, lacking the sensorimotor grounding that connects human concepts to the world. LLMs inherit a variant of this problem: their outputs are shaped entirely by statistical regularities in text, without causal contact with the phenomena those outputs purport to describe.

The Chinese Room and Its Successors. Searle’s famous thought experiment (Searle, 1980) challenged the sufficiency of syntactic manipulation for genuine understanding. While subsequent debate has refined (and contested) this intuition, the core question persists: what distinguishes systems that merely process information from those that genuinely comprehend it?

Stochastic Parrots. Bender et al. (2021) provocatively characterized LLMs as “stochastic parrots”—systems that produce plausible-seeming text without understanding its meaning. This framing has been nuanced (Mitchell and Krakauer, 2023; Shanahan, 2024), but it highlights the fundamental uncertainty about the epistemic status of LLM outputs.

Inferentialism and the Space of Reasons. From a Sellarsian-Brandomian perspective, Sambrotta (2025) argue that LLMs follow statistical patterns rather than genuine inferential norms—they can appear to reason without inhabiting the “logical space of reasons.” The present paper provides empirical illustration of this philosophical claim.

Understanding vs. Mere Explanation. Epistemologists have increasingly distinguished understanding from knowledge, arguing that understanding involves grasping explanatory connections rather than merely possessing true beliefs (Grimm, 2012; Elgin, 2017). This distinction becomes crucial when evaluating AI systems: even if an LLM’s outputs happen to be correct, does the underlying process exhibit the structural features associated with understanding why?

These debates remain largely theoretical. This paper contributes empirical evidence by documenting a specific phenomenon—the Coherence Paradox—that bears directly on two influential assumptions in contemporary AI research.

Recent discussions in Minds and Machines and related venues have increasingly framed AI systems as epistemic agents whose outputs invite normative evaluation rather than mere performance benchmarking. Questions of epistemic authority, reliability, and justified trust now accompany assessments of capability. The present paper contributes to this debate by examining whether coherence, grounding, and competence align in ways that would warrant attributing understanding or epistemic credit to artificial systems.

1.3 Two Assumptions Under Challenge

The Coherence-Reliability Assumption. A central premise in interpretability research is that explanation quality serves as a proxy for model reliability. Rudin (2019) argues that interpretable models—those providing coherent, human-understandable explanations—should be preferred in high-stakes domains precisely because their transparency enables justified trust. This assumption rests on an implicit correlation: systems generating coherent explanations thereby exhibit valid reasoning processes. When an LLM articulates why a particular action should succeed, interpretability frameworks treat this as evidence that the system grasps relevant causal structure.

But what if coherent explanations systematically diverge from actual causal mechanisms? If systems can generate compelling reasoning while being fundamentally wrong about why their recommendations work, explanation quality cannot serve as a reliable indicator of reasoning validity.

The Behavioral Competence Assumption. Recent debate about LLM capabilities centers on whether behavioral competence indicates genuine understanding. Bubeck et al. (2023) argue that GPT-4 exhibits “sparks of artificial general intelligence,” pointing to its ability to generate contextually appropriate responses across diverse domains. As Mitchell and Krakauer (2023) note, the debate often hinges on what counts as evidence for “understanding.”

These optimistic interpretations share a methodological assumption: systems exhibiting coherent, contextually-sensitive outputs thereby demonstrate some form of genuine comprehension. But what if correct outcomes can be achieved through mechanisms the system fundamentally misidentifies? And what if correct diagnoses fail to translate into effective action? If coherence and competence can dissociate in both directions, neither alone suffices as evidence for understanding.

The empirical findings presented in this paper suggest that both dissociations occur—and that they occur systematically depending on epistemic conditions. I call this phenomenon the Coherence Paradox.

1.4 The Coherence Paradox

More precisely, I define the Coherence Paradox as follows:

Coherence Paradox: The phenomenon in which an epistemic agent’s internally consistent explanations systematically diverge from empirical reality, such that greater explanatory coherence may obscure rather than reveal the agent’s actual epistemic relationship to the domain.

The paradox has two components. First, coherence and grounding are separable: a system can produce logically consistent explanations that correctly connect observations to hypotheses to actions, while being entirely wrong about the actual causal mechanisms at work. Second, this separation may be systematic rather than occasional: the very capabilities that enable fluent explanation may be independent of—or even inversely related to—genuine understanding.

Why call this a paradox rather than merely a dissociation? The term is warranted because the phenomenon violates a widely held assumption: that coherent explanation reliably indicates epistemic contact with reality. Mere dissociation would mean coherence and grounding are independent. What I document is stronger: their relationship inverts depending on epistemic regime. In low-observability domains, greater coherence accompanies less grounding. In high-observability domains, greater grounding accompanies less effective action. This bidirectional inversion is paradoxical because it contradicts a deeply held intuition: that explanation quality and epistemic reliability should covary positively. This intuition is embedded in both folk epistemology and AI evaluation practice.

A clarification: this is an epistemic paradox, not a causal one. I do not claim that observability causes the inversion in a strict interventionist sense. Rather, the paradox is structural: across epistemic regimes that differ in observability, the coherence-grounding relationship takes opposite signs. The philosophical interest lies in this structural pattern, not in isolating observability as a causal variable.

If the Coherence Paradox is real, it has profound implications: explanation quality cannot serve as a reliable proxy for reasoning validity, and improvements in LLM explanatory capabilities may paradoxically increase the risk of epistemic deception. This raises a deeper question: what criteria could distinguish genuine understanding from sophisticated confabulation? The remainder of this paper develops the conceptual tools to address this question and provides empirical evidence that the paradox is indeed real—and bidirectional.

1.5 Contributions and Structure

This paper makes four contributions:

  1. 1.

    Conceptual. I formalize the Observability Gap and introduce the Bidirectional Coherence Paradox: the phenomenon whereby the coherence-grounding relationship not only dissociates but inverts across observability regimes.

  2. 2.

    Empirical. Through controlled experiments in two domains (compiler optimization, hyperparameter tuning), I document a 61-percentage-point swing. In the low-observability domain: +31pp (actions succeed, explanations fail). In the high-observability domain: –30pp (explanations succeed, actions fail). This effect is statistically robust (Mann-Whitney p<0.0001p<0.0001, 95% CI [33.1, 91.3]pp), though its generalization beyond these specific domains remains to be established. Crucially, these domains were selected for their epistemic proximity to physical reality: success is determined by hardware behavior and numerical dynamics, not by linguistic convention or semantic agreement.

  3. 3.

    Theoretical. I propose the Epistemic Triangle model, which explains how observability determines whether prior-dominated or signal-dominated reasoning prevails, producing qualitatively different failure modes.

  4. 4.

    Philosophical. I draw implications for debates on epistemic luck, the coherentism/foundationalism debate, the Rylean knowing-that/knowing-how distinction, and the conditions for attributing understanding to artificial systems. I propose integrated justification—a tripartite framework requiring coherence, grounding, and a proper basing relation—as a minimal standard for evaluating artificial epistemic agents.

The paper unfolds as follows. Section 2 develops the conceptual framework. Section 3 describes the empirical methodology. Section 4 presents the bidirectional paradox findings. Section 5 develops the Epistemic Triangle model. Section 6 explores philosophical implications. Section 7 concludes.

2 Conceptual Framework: Coherence, Grounding, and Understanding

Before presenting empirical findings, I establish the conceptual vocabulary required to interpret them. This section develops the key constructs—observability, coherence, grounding, understanding—that structure the analysis.

2.1 Terminological Clarification

This paper employs epistemic vocabulary—“understanding,” “grounding,” “coherence”—when discussing LLM outputs. A clarification of register is necessary.

I adopt what might be called epistemic functionalism: terms like “grounded” and “coherent” are applied literally, not metaphorically, but their application conditions are functional rather than phenomenological. An explanation is grounded if and only if its stated causal mechanism matches observable metric changes; it is coherent if and only if its inferential structure is internally consistent. These are objective, measurable properties of outputs—not attributions of inner experience.

Grounding is not introduced here as a merely descriptive alignment between explanations and metrics, but as a functional epistemic notion with normative force: an explanation is grounded if it tracks the actual causal structure of the domain as revealed through available interventions and observations.11 1 This is the same sense in which grounding is attributed to scientific models. Consider a climate model: it is grounded not because atmospheric dynamics are directly observable at all scales, but because its predictions systematically track observable outcomes under intervention. Grounding requires experimental validation, not direct mechanistic access. The same standard applies here: LLM explanations are grounded when their causal claims systematically predict metric changes under the interventions those claims recommend.

This approach follows Dennett (1987): one may apply intentional vocabulary to systems when doing so enables systematic prediction and explanation of behavior. This does not commit one to claims about phenomenal consciousness. The question is not whether LLMs “really” understand in some metaphysically privileged sense, but whether their outputs satisfy the functional criteria used to attribute understanding in practice. If outputs satisfy some criteria while failing others, this may reveal something important about the structure of those criteria themselves.

When I speak of “epistemic luck” or “basing relations,” I am asking: if one applies standard epistemological frameworks to LLM outputs, what does one find? The answer—that outputs can satisfy coherence criteria while failing grounding criteria, or vice versa—is informative regardless of whether one thinks the epistemic vocabulary applies “genuinely” or merely “as-if.” The bidirectional paradox is a structural finding about the dissociability of functional properties; its philosophical significance does not depend on resolving debates about machine consciousness.

2.2 The Observability Gap

Valid causal inference requires access to the factors that actually determine outcomes. When an agent reasons about a domain, its conclusions can only be as reliable as the information available to it (Floridi, 2011). I define the Observability Gap as:

Observability Gap: The discrepancy between the causal information required for valid inference and the information actually available through observable signals.

Formally, let 𝒞\mathcal{C} denote the set of true causal factors determining system behavior, and let 𝒪\mathcal{O} denote the set of observable proxies available to the reasoning agent. The Observability Gap can be characterized as:

Gap​(𝒞,𝒪)=1−I⁡(𝒪,𝒞)H⁡(𝒞)\text{Gap}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{O})=1-\frac{I(\mathcal{O};\mathcal{C})}{H(\mathcal{C})} (1)

where I⁡(𝒪,𝒞)I(\mathcal{O};\mathcal{C}) is the mutual information between observables and causal factors, and H⁡(𝒞)H(\mathcal{C}) is the entropy of the causal factors. When Gap≈0\text{Gap}\approx 0, observables fully determine causal states and valid inference is possible. When Gap≈1\text{Gap}\approx 1, observables provide negligible information about true causes.

The Observability Gap is not merely a practical limitation but an epistemic condition that fundamentally constrains what can be known. When the gap is large, no amount of sophisticated reasoning can compensate for missing information. This has important implications for understanding: if understanding requires grasping causal structure, and causal structure is unobservable, then genuine understanding may be impossible regardless of how coherent the agent’s explanations appear.

2.3 Abductive Reasoning and Inference to the Best Explanation

Following Peirce’s formulation (Peirce, 1877), I frame the reasoning process as abductive inference: reasoning from observed effects to hypothesized causes. Unlike deduction (which derives necessary conclusions) or induction (which generalizes from instances), abduction operates under fundamental uncertainty—multiple hypotheses may explain the same observations.

Lipton (2004) distinguishes between explanations that are “lovely”—elegant, unifying, simple—and explanations that are “likely”—probably true. This distinction is crucial for analyzing LLM outputs. LLMs are trained to produce text that humans find compelling, optimizing for loveliness rather than likelihood. A lovely explanation satisfies cognitive preferences for coherence and simplicity. A likely explanation correctly identifies actual causes.

The Coherence Paradox can be characterized as a systematic divergence between loveliness and likelihood: LLM architectures may excel at generating lovely explanations that are not likely to be true.

2.4 Coherence, Grounding, and Pragmatic Competence

I distinguish three dimensions of reasoning quality:

Coherence measures the internal logical consistency of a reasoning chain. A coherent explanation connects observations to hypotheses to actions through valid inferential steps. High coherence means the reasoning “makes sense” given stated premises. Coherence is a syntactic property: it can be assessed without reference to external reality.

Grounding measures the correspondence between the reasoning chain and physical reality. A grounded explanation makes correct, testable interventional predictions about observable outcomes; when observables are sufficiently informative, this also provides evidence that the explanation tracks the underlying causal mechanism. Grounding is a semantic property: it requires comparing the explanation to facts about the world. In Ryle’s terms, grounding corresponds to knowing-that—propositional knowledge of why a system behaves as it does (Ryle, 1984).

Pragmatic competence measures whether the system’s chosen interventions actually improve outcomes, regardless of whether its explanations are correct. A pragmatically competent system selects effective actions even if it cannot articulate why they work. This corresponds to Ryle’s knowing-how—the capacity for effective performance that need not be accompanied by articulable propositional knowledge.

Crucially, coherence is the surface property shared by both grounded and competent outputs. Whether the LLM is acting on transferred heuristics (knowing-how without knowing-that) or correctly diagnosing a problem it cannot solve (knowing-that without knowing-how), its explanations appear equally coherent. Coherence is what makes both failure modes invisible from the outside. The Coherence Paradox is precisely this: coherence obscures the dissociation between grounding and competence rather than revealing it.

The distinction maps onto classic debates in epistemology. Coherentist theories of justification hold that beliefs are justified by their coherence with other beliefs (BonJour, 1985; Rescher, 1973). Foundationalist theories require some beliefs to be justified by direct contact with reality. The Coherence Paradox suggests that neither is sufficient: a system can be internally coherent while systematically disconnected from the world (Type A), or well-grounded in observable reality while unable to act effectively on that grounding (Type B). Ryle’s distinction between knowing-that and knowing-how, long debated in epistemology and philosophy of mind, here receives an unexpected empirical illustration: LLMs can exhibit one without the other, and coherence masks which one they possess.

2.5 Functional Criteria for Understanding

Recent epistemology has emphasized that understanding is not reducible to knowledge (Grimm, 2012; Elgin, 2017; Zagzebski, 2001). Understanding involves grasping explanatory connections—seeing why things are as they are, not merely that they are. When applied to artificial systems, this framework suggests functional criteria that outputs might or might not satisfy:

  • •

    A system might produce correct outputs without its processing exhibiting the structural features associated with understanding why those outputs are correct.

  • •

    A system might generate coherent explanations without those explanations being grounded in actual causal mechanisms.

  • •

    Even if both outputs and explanations happen to be correct, the system might fail to exhibit understanding if it cannot reliably distinguish contexts where its patterns apply from those where they fail.

Elgin (2017) argues that understanding is “true enough”—it need not be perfectly accurate but must capture the relevant structure. This criterion is useful but incomplete: how does one assess whether an artificial system’s outputs capture “relevant structure” when one cannot directly inspect its internal representations?

The approach developed here offers a partial answer: I empirically measure the gap between coherence and grounding, providing evidence about whether the system’s outputs track reality or merely satisfy internal consistency constraints. This is an assessment of functional properties, not an attribution of mental states.

From explanation to understanding. One might ask: why does this bear on understanding rather than merely on explanation quality? The answer is that the criteria employed here are deliberately minimal. If a system fails even to track observable metric changes (low ASR), it cannot satisfy any robust criterion for understanding the domain. If it tracks metrics but cannot translate diagnosis into effective action (Type B), it fails the pragmatic test that understanding should enable successful intervention. If it succeeds in action but confabulates mechanisms (Type A), it fails the explanatory test that understanding requires grasping why actions work. These are not demanding philosophical criteria—they are baseline functional requirements. That LLMs fail them systematically, in different directions depending on observability, suggests that the disconnect between explanation and understanding is not occasional but structural.

2.6 Confabulation and Post-Hoc Rationalization

Neuropsychological research has documented confabulation: patients with certain brain lesions produce plausible-sounding explanations for behaviors they did not actually perform for the reasons they cite (Hirstein, 2005). Importantly, confabulating patients are not lying—they genuinely believe their explanations. The explanations are coherent, confidently delivered, and domain-appropriate; they are simply false.

Nisbett and Wilson (1977) demonstrated that even healthy humans routinely confabulate, producing explanations for their choices that do not reflect actual decision processes. When asked why they preferred one item over another, subjects generated plausible reasons that post-hoc investigation revealed to be fabricated.

LLM outputs may exhibit a structural analog of confabulation—generating plausible explanations disconnected from actual causal processes. Given a prompt requesting explanation, a model returns statistically probable text without access to the causal mechanisms it purports to describe. Probability is assessed relative to training data distributions, not physical reality. An architecture optimized for plausibility systematically generates coherent but ungrounded explanations.

This connects to Miller (2019)’s observation that humans prefer explanations that are contrastive, selective, and socially tailored—and LLMs excel at generating text with these surface features. But Miller’s analysis focuses on explanation as a communicative act, not on whether the generating architecture has access to causal structure. Similarly, Lipton (2018) notes that interpretability conflates multiple desiderata: transparency, justification, and actionable guidance. LLM-generated text may satisfy some of these goals while failing others.

The conceptual framework is now in place. The next section describes the empirical methodology for testing whether coherence and grounding actually dissociate in LLM reasoning.

3 Empirical Methodology

To investigate the Coherence Paradox empirically, I developed a diagnostic framework for probing reasoning under controlled epistemic limitations. The goal is not to benchmark LLM performance—this is not a machine learning paper measuring which model optimizes best. Rather, the goal is to test epistemological assumptions: does coherent explanation reliably indicate grounded reasoning? The empirical apparatus serves philosophical inquiry, using controlled domains to expose structural features of the coherence-grounding relationship. Full technical details appear in Appendix A.

3.1 Design Principles and Domain Selection

The methodology requires three properties: (1) controlled observability—the domain must have a known, measurable gap between observable signals and true causal factors; (2) structured explanation—the LLM must produce explicit reasoning chains, not just outputs; and (3) empirical verification—it must be possible to independently verify whether the LLM’s causal claims match reality.

3.1.1 Epistemic Proximity to Physical Reality

Domain selection was driven by epistemic proximity to physical reality, not convenience or benchmark coverage. Both compiler optimization and neural network training involve interventions whose success is determined by non-linguistic, non-social causal mechanisms—hardware behavior, numerical stability, and physical execution.

These domains minimize interpretive slack: improvements are not a matter of semantic agreement or task framing, but of whether code runs faster or training converges. There is no plausible sense in which a compiler or a loss surface “understands” a task. If epistemic pathologies arise here, they arise in the absence of psychological or semantic confounds.

This design choice is philosophically motivated. If coherence and grounding come apart even in domains tightly coupled to hardware-level reality, the dissociation cannot be attributed to linguistic ambiguity or anthropomorphic projection. It reflects a structural feature of how current systems integrate priors and signals.

Table 1 summarizes the key properties of the selected domains.

3.1.2 The Two Domains

I selected two domains at opposite ends of the observability spectrum:

Low Observability: Compiler Optimization. Hardware performance counters (IPC, cache miss rates) are noisy proxies for microarchitectural phenomena. The LLM observes aggregated metrics but cannot directly see prefetcher behavior, pipeline dynamics, or instruction scheduling. This creates a large Observability Gap where valid causal inference is difficult.

High Observability: Hyperparameter Optimization. Neural network training provides direct access to loss values, gradient norms, and convergence rates. The causal relationship between hyperparameters and outcomes is more transparent—when learning rate is too high, loss diverges observably.

3.2 Operationalizing Competence and Grounding

The conceptual framework distinguishes three dimensions: coherence, grounding, and pragmatic competence (Section 2.4). The empirical apparatus operationalizes these as follows:

Action Success Rate (ActSR) operationalizes pragmatic competence: it measures whether the LLM’s chosen intervention improves outcomes, regardless of whether its explanation is correct. High ActSR indicates effective knowing-how—the system acts well.

Abductive Success Rate (ASR) operationalizes functional grounding: it measures whether the LLM’s stated hypothesis matches observed changes. If the LLM claims “reducing learning rate will stabilize training” and stability metrics improve, ASR credits the explanation as grounded. High ASR indicates effective knowing-that—the system diagnoses correctly.

Coherence is not separately measured because it is a constant: the LLM’s structured output format enforces internally consistent reasoning chains in every iteration. Coherence is the surface that both metrics share. The philosophical interest lies in what coherence conceals: whether the system’s coherent outputs reflect genuine grounding, genuine competence, both, or neither.

The gap ActSR−ASR\text{ActSR}-\text{ASR} quantifies the Coherence Paradox: positive gaps indicate competence without grounding (knowing-how without knowing-that); negative gaps indicate grounding without competence (knowing-that without knowing-how). In both cases, coherence is maintained, making the dissociation invisible to any evaluation that relies on explanation quality alone.

3.3 Methodological Limitations of ASR

The ASR metric functions as a proxy for interventional traceability rather than a direct measure of full causal identification. False positives arise when metrics change coincidentally; false negatives occur when correct mechanisms operate below measurement granularity; and metric selection effects introduce systematic bias. These limitations affect absolute ASR values more than comparative findings: the 61-percentage-point swing reflects a real difference even if absolute values carry ±\pm10–15pp uncertainty. The qualitative finding—that the gap inverts—is robust to plausible measurement error.

A skeptic might object that ASR captures functional grounding (correct interventional predictions) rather than genuine causal grounding. This is partly right: ASR is weaker than full symbol–world grounding. But for black-box systems, functional grounding is the only grounding we can assess—the same standard applied to scientific models. The philosophical point is this: if even this minimal criterion fails systematically (Type A) or succeeds without enabling effective action (Type B), stronger notions of grounding will not rescue explanation-based trust. If a system cannot even track metrics it directly observes, debates about “deep” grounding are moot. A fuller discussion of measurement limitations appears in Appendix A.

3.4 Alternative Explanations

Several non-observability factors might contribute to domain differences: action space structure (12 vs. 24 options), prior strength asymmetry (decades of compiler folklore vs. heterogeneous HPO practices), domain complexity, autoregressive generation biases, and task difficulty asymmetry. These deserve careful consideration.

The most natural objection—that HPO is simply harder to execute but easier to diagnose—conflates absolute performance with the correlation structure. If HPO were uniformly harder, both metrics should degrade. Instead, we observe selective improvement in ASR (90% vs. 41%) coupled with degradation in ActSR (60% vs. 72%). This inversion—not the absolute values—constitutes the paradox. Similarly, action space size alone cannot explain the inversion: larger spaces would predict uniform degradation, not opposite movements on the two metrics.

These alternatives are not mutually exclusive with the observability hypothesis; they may represent mechanisms through which observability exerts its effects. The contribution is not to establish observability as the only factor but to document that the coherence-grounding relationship can invert. This study employs a quasi-experimental design: observability was not manipulated while holding other factors constant. The claim is therefore that observability covaries with paradox type in a pattern consistent with the Epistemic Triangle, not that it causes the inversion in a strict interventionist sense. Future work might approach causal identification through within-domain manipulation (e.g., artificially degrading signal quality in HPO). A detailed discussion of each alternative explanation appears in Appendix A.

4 The Bidirectional Coherence Paradox

The central empirical finding is that the coherence-grounding relationship not only dissociates but inverts across observability regimes. This bidirectional pattern reveals that coherence and grounding can be systematically opposed, not merely independent.

4.1 Type A: Coherent Without Grounding (Low Observability)

In the compiler optimization domain, where hardware counters provide only indirect signals about microarchitectural behavior, I observe:

  • •

    Action Success Rate (ActSR): 72%

  • •

    Abductive Success Rate (ASR): 41%

  • •

    Gap: +31 percentage points

The positive gap indicates that the LLM’s actions succeed far more often than its explanations are correct.

Illustrative Case. Over 10 iterations on the jacobi-2d benchmark, performance improved overall while the hypothesized causal metric (L1 cache miss rate) remained flat.22 2 Best speedup reached 1.0127×\times; L1 miss rate stayed within ∼\sim22.17–22.18% throughout all iterations. The LLM’s hypothesis—“reduce cache misses via vectorization”—was internally coherent but empirically ungrounded. The actual improvement arose from unmeasured factors, likely prefetcher efficiency or instruction-level parallelism.

This pattern exemplifies epistemic luck in action: correct outcomes achieved through mechanisms the system does not understand (Pritchard, 2005). Section 6 develops the philosophical implications.

4.2 Type B: Grounded Without Success (High Observability)

In the hyperparameter optimization domain, where the LLM directly observes loss values, gradient norms, and convergence rates, the pattern inverts:

  • •

    Action Success Rate (ActSR): 60%

  • •

    Abductive Success Rate (ASR): 90%

  • •

    Gap: –30 percentage points

The negative gap indicates that the LLM’s explanations are grounded far more often than its actions succeed. When the model states “SGD is causing training instability due to high gradient variance,” gradient metrics typically confirm this diagnosis. Yet the chosen intervention (e.g., gradient clipping) often fails to improve outcomes.

Illustrative Case. In iteration 3 of the HPO experiment, the LLM correctly diagnosed that switching to SGD had caused instability---gradient norms had spiked and loss variance increased. The explanation was grounded: the diagnosed mechanism matched observed metrics. However, the chosen action (enabling gradient clipping at 1.0) failed to resolve the issue.33 3 Validation loss worsened from 0.77 to 1.17, a 52% regression despite the correct diagnosis.

This pattern represents a dissociation between diagnosis and intervention: correct identification of causal structure does not translate into effective action.

Figure 1 illustrates both paradox types through representative case studies.

4.3 The 61-Point Swing: Statistical Validation

The difference between domains is not merely directional but massive in magnitude:

  • •

    Observed difference: 61 percentage points (+31pp vs –30pp)

  • •

    Bootstrap 95% CI: [33.1, 91.3] pp

  • •

    Mann-Whitney U: 100.0, p<0.0001p<0.0001

Figure 2 provides direct visual comparison of the two paradox types.

This swing is not explicable by random variation or measurement error. The bootstrap 95% confidence interval [33.1, 91.3]pp excludes zero by a wide margin, and the Mann-Whitney test confirms significance (p<0.0001p<0.0001). The bidirectional pattern suggests that coherence and grounding can be inversely related depending on epistemic conditions—at least in these two domains, under these experimental constraints, with this particular architecture.

Scope of the claim. The 61-point swing is an empirical finding in two specific domains selected to represent opposite ends of an observability spectrum. Whether this pattern generalizes to intermediate-observability domains, to other LLM architectures, or to domains with different prior structures remains an open question. What the data establish is that the coherence-grounding relationship can invert—not that it must invert whenever observability changes. The contribution of this paper is to demonstrate the structural possibility of such inversion. Establishing possibility suffices to challenge the widespread assumption that coherence reliably signals grounding, even if the prevalence of this pattern across domains remains to be determined.

5 The Epistemic Triangle: A Theoretical Model

The bidirectional paradox demands theoretical explanation. Why does low observability produce coherent-but-ungrounded reasoning, while high observability produces grounded-but-ineffective reasoning? I propose the Epistemic Triangle model to explain this inversion (Figure 3).

5.1 The Three Vertices

LLM reasoning integrates three distinct information sources:

Weak Signals (Observational). Observable metrics provide the system’s only direct window into the domain. In low-observability regimes, these signals are noisy aggregates that lose fine-grained causal information. They constrain but do not determine valid inference.

Strong Priors (Experiential). The LLM’s training corpus encodes patterns about domain structures.44 4 Examples include: “nested loops with small bodies benefit from unrolling,” “high cache miss rates suggest memory-bound behavior,” “SGD generalizes better than Adam.” These priors are not learned from the current task but transferred from training. They represent crystallized expertise—or crystallized bias.

Domain Knowledge (Semantic). General knowledge about the domain provides interpretive scaffolding: compiler semantics, architectural principles, pragmatic constraints. This knowledge enables the construction of coherent narratives that connect observations to actions.

5.2 Explaining the Bidirectional Paradox

The Epistemic Triangle explains why the coherence-grounding relationship inverts across observability regimes:

Type A (Low Observability): Prior-Dominated Processing. When Weak Signals provide minimal information, Strong Priors dominate output generation. The model’s training encodes that cache misses correlate with memory bottlenecks (Domain Knowledge) and that vectorization addresses them (Strong Prior). It generates coherent narratives from these statistical associations regardless of whether observations confirm them. Actions succeed because priors encode genuine heuristics. Explanations fail because actual mechanisms are unobservable.

Type B (High Observability): Signal-Dominated Processing. When Weak Signals become informative, they dominate over Strong Priors. The model receives direct signals that loss is diverging or gradients are exploding. Explanations succeed because the causal structure is observable. But action selection requires more than diagnosis—it requires selecting which intervention will be effective. Strong Priors for HPO are less reliable than for compiler optimization: the action space is less constrained, interactions more complex. The model generates correct diagnoses but selects suboptimal interventions.

The Inversion Mechanism. The key insight is that observability differentially affects grounding versus action selection. High observability directly improves grounding—explanations can be verified against observable signals—but may not improve action selection. Correct diagnosis does not determine optimal intervention. Low observability impairs grounding (explanations cannot be verified) but may not impair action selection if strong priors encode effective heuristics.

This account is offered as a candidate explanation for the observed pattern, not as a verified causal mechanism. The Epistemic Triangle provides a framework for understanding how observability might produce bidirectional effects, but the data do not definitively establish that this is the operative mechanism rather than some alternative (see Section 3.4). The model’s value lies in generating testable predictions for future work:

Falsifiable predictions. The Epistemic Triangle generates three testable predictions. (1) Intermediate observability, intermediate gap: Domains with moderate observability (e.g., database query optimization) should exhibit ActSR-ASR gaps between +31pp and –30pp. (2) Prior strength modulates Type A magnitude: Within low-observability domains, those with weaker training priors should show smaller positive gaps, as prior-dominated success depends on prior quality. (3) Action space complexity modulates Type B magnitude: Within high-observability domains, simpler action spaces should show smaller negative gaps, as diagnosis-to-action translation becomes easier. These predictions are falsifiable: if intermediate domains show extreme gaps, or if prior strength and action complexity do not modulate as predicted, the Epistemic Triangle would require revision or rejection.

5.3 Visualizing the Observability Spectrum

Figure 4 synthesizes how the Epistemic Triangle predicts different failure modes across the observability spectrum.

The Epistemic Triangle provides a theoretical account of the bidirectional paradox. The next section explores its philosophical implications for epistemology and debates on machine understanding.

6 Philosophical Implications

The bidirectional Coherence Paradox has significant implications for epistemology and debates on machine understanding. I focus on four interconnected themes that emerge directly from the empirical findings.

6.1 Epistemic Luck and the Type A Paradox

The Type A pattern—correct actions with incorrect explanations—instantiates what epistemologists call epistemic luck (Pritchard, 2005). In Gettier-style cases, an agent holds a true belief that fails to constitute knowledge because the connection between belief and truth is accidental. The Type A Paradox presents an analogous structure: the system achieves correct outcomes through mechanisms disconnected from its generated explanations.

Consider the jacobi-2d case: the vectorization recommendation improved performance, but not through the hypothesized mechanism (reduced cache misses). The success was veridically lucky—the action happened to be correct despite the faulty explanation. Applying epistemic vocabulary, this would not constitute knowledge in any robust sense; it is fortunate pattern-matching dressed in the clothing of explanation.

Sosa (2007) distinguishes between apt performance (success through competence) and mere accurate performance (success by luck). The Type A Paradox reveals that LLM outputs can be accurate without being apt: they hit the target without exhibiting the structural features typically associated with genuine skill. This distinction matters for trust—one should not rely on systems whose successes are systematically lucky. As Ferrario et al. (2024) argue from a virtue epistemology perspective, predictive accuracy does not confer epistemic authority. Genuine expertise requires a relationship with understanding that current AI systems do not satisfy.

6.2 Understanding Without Competence and the Type B Paradox

The Type B pattern poses a different philosophical puzzle: how can a system generate correct diagnoses yet fail to select effective interventions? This challenges the intuition that diagnostic accuracy is sufficient for successful intervention.

One resolution invokes the distinction between theoretical and practical knowledge. A system may generate outputs that correctly identify a problem (that SGD causes instability) without generating outputs that correctly solve it. Aristotelian phronesis—practical wisdom—requires not just pattern-matching on problem descriptions but selecting appropriate responses in particular circumstances. The Type B Paradox suggests that the LLM possesses something analogous to theoria (contemplative knowledge of what is the case) without phronesis (the practical capacity to act well in context). This is not merely a quantitative deficit—needing “more” knowledge—but a qualitative gap between two distinct epistemic capacities.

This gap has a structural explanation. Diagnosis requires identifying which known pattern matches the observed data—a recognition task well-suited to statistical pattern-matching. Prescription requires selecting among interventions whose outcomes depend on complex, context-specific interactions that may not be well-represented in training data. The asymmetry between these tasks is not accidental but architectural: the transformer architecture excels at pattern recognition across its training distribution while lacking the capacity for the kind of counterfactual simulation that effective intervention demands.

Alternatively, the Type B Paradox may reveal that diagnosis and prescription are distinct functional capacities more generally. Medical diagnosticians can identify diseases they cannot treat; engineers can diagnose failures they cannot repair. The human case, however, differs in a crucial respect: a skilled diagnostician who cannot treat a disease knows that she cannot treat it, and can refer the patient accordingly. The LLM exhibits no such metacognitive boundary—it prescribes with the same confidence whether or not its interventions are likely to succeed. This absence of calibrated self-assessment compounds the Type B failure: not only does grounding fail to produce competence, but the system cannot signal when this failure is occurring.

6.3 The Basing Relation and Its Absence in LLMs

Epistemologists have long recognized that knowledge requires more than true belief plus justification—the belief must be based on the justification. This basing relation (Korcz, 2000) connects a belief to its justificatory grounds. I know that pp not merely when I believe pp truly and have evidence for pp, but when my belief is held because of that evidence. A student who gives the correct answer while ignoring the teacher’s explanation does not know, even if the answer is right and the explanation sound.

The bidirectional paradox reveals that LLM outputs systematically lack proper basing relations. The Type A Paradox shows correct actions generated without connection to correct explanations—the system succeeds despite faulty explanations, not because of sound ones. The Type B Paradox shows correct diagnoses without connection to effective interventions—accurate problem identification fails to translate into successful resolution. In both cases, the “because of” relation fails.

This analysis clarifies why simple criteria for attributing understanding are insufficient. Behavioral competence (producing correct outputs) fails: Type A shows success without proper basing. Explanatory accuracy (producing grounded explanations) fails: Type B shows grounding without proper basing. Even their conjunction may be insufficient if the connection between explanation and action is accidental rather than constitutive. Understanding requires integrated competence: correct actions that flow from correct explanations through a reliable basing relation.

6.4 Coherentism, Foundationalism, and the Bidirectional Challenge

The bidirectional paradox complicates the classical debate between coherentist and foundationalist theories of justification in unexpected ways.

Against Pure Coherentism. The Type A Paradox shows that coherence is insufficient: the LLM produces internally consistent reasoning chains while only 41% of its hypotheses match reality. A system can be internally coherent while systematically disconnected from the world. This supports foundationalist critiques of coherentism (BonJour, 1985).

Against Pure Foundationalism. But the Type B Paradox complicates the foundationalist response. Here, grounding in observable reality does not suffice for epistemic success. The LLM’s explanations are grounded (90% ASR) yet its actions often fail (60% ActSR). Having foundations—direct access to causal information—does not guarantee practical knowledge. Knowing-that does not entail knowing-how.

The Bidirectional Challenge. Neither pure coherentism nor pure foundationalism captures the epistemology of artificial reasoning:

  • •

    Coherentism fails in low-observability regimes (Type A): coherent but ungrounded.

  • •

    Foundationalism fails in high-observability regimes (Type B): grounded but ineffective.

Beyond Foundherentism. Haack (1993) anticipated the inadequacy of both pure positions and proposed foundherentism: a hybrid view in which beliefs are justified by both experiential grounding and mutual coherence, much as entries in a crossword puzzle are supported by both clues (experience) and interlocking answers (coherence). Foundherentism is closer to what the data demand than either pure alternative.

However, it remains insufficient for the present case. Haack’s framework addresses the relationship between coherence and grounding—how beliefs can be supported simultaneously by experiential foundations and by their fit with other beliefs. The crossword analogy is apt: a good answer fits both the clue (grounding) and the intersecting letters (coherence). But the analogy assumes that fitting the clue and fitting the intersections are jointly sufficient for a correct answer. The bidirectional paradox reveals a dimension that the crossword analogy does not capture: the relationship between knowing what the answer is and being able to use that answer productively. A crossword solver who fills in the correct word but cannot use it in a sentence has not understood the word—she has merely completed a pattern.

What the bidirectional paradox reveals, then, is a third dimension that neither coherentism, foundationalism, nor foundherentism explicitly addresses: the basing relation connecting explanation to action. Foundherentism reunites coherence and grounding; but it does not require that the justified belief guide effective intervention. The Type B Paradox shows precisely this gap: a system whose beliefs are both coherent and grounded (in Haack’s sense), yet whose actions are not properly based on those beliefs. The crossword is filled in correctly, but the solver cannot use the words.

Integrated Justification. I propose that adequate epistemic evaluation of artificial agents requires a tripartite structure:

  1. 1.

    Coherence: the system’s reasoning is internally consistent.

  2. 2.

    Grounding: the system’s explanations track observable causal structure (knowing-that).

  3. 3.

    Basing: the system’s actions flow from its explanations through a reliable connection—correct actions are taken because of correct understanding, not merely alongside it (knowing-how connected to knowing-that).

I term this conjunction integrated justification. The concept draws on Ryle’s distinction between knowing-that and knowing-how (Ryle, 1984), but adds a structural requirement: genuine understanding requires not merely possessing both, but that they be connected through a proper basing relation (Korcz, 2000). A system that knows-that and knows-how independently—as LLMs appear to do—does not genuinely understand, because its competence is not grounded in its knowledge. The “because of” relation is absent.

A Taxonomy of Epistemic Failures. The tripartite structure generates a taxonomy of failure modes, of which the bidirectional paradox documents two:

Profile (d)—tacit expertise—is philosophically notable and deserves closer examination. It describes an agent that reliably acts well because of its experience, but cannot articulate why. This is the master craftsman who “just knows” where to strike the chisel, the experienced clinician whose diagnoses outstrip her ability to explain them, the chess grandmaster who “sees” the right move before calculating variations. As Polanyi famously put it, “we can know more than we can tell” (Polanyi, 1966), which is precisely the structure of tacit knowledge.

LLMs exhibit the structural inverse of tacit expertise. The craftsman has basing without coherence: her actions flow reliably from her experience, but she cannot articulate the connection. The LLM has coherence without basing: it always articulates, fluently and confidently, but the articulation is disconnected from the basis of its action. They are, in a precise sense, the anti-craftsman: all explanation, no tacit grounding.

This inversion is not merely a curiosity. It reveals something important about the epistemic architecture of current LLMs. Human tacit expertise is opaque from the inside—the expert cannot introspect on her own competence. LLM competence is opaque from the outside—the system generates articulate explanations that obscure the actual basis of its performance. The opacity is symmetrical but inverted: the craftsman’s silence is epistemically honest (she knows she cannot explain), while the LLM’s fluency is epistemically misleading (it generates explanations regardless of whether they track its actual processing). This suggests that in human-AI collaboration, the tacit expert and the articulate LLM may be complementary—but only if users recognize that the LLM’s explanatory fluency is not evidence of the kind of grounded competence that the tacit expert possesses silently.

Necessity and Sufficiency. What the data establish is that each component is necessary: the absence of grounding produces Type A failures; the absence of basing produces Type B failures; and coherence alone, always present in LLM outputs, is demonstrably insufficient. Whether the three components are jointly sufficient for genuine understanding cannot be established from two domains. It remains possible that further conditions—temporal persistence, counterfactual sensitivity, self-correction under feedback—are also required. The tripartite structure is offered as a minimal framework: these three components are necessary, and their conjunction is a reasonable candidate for sufficiency pending further investigation.

The bidirectional paradox thus reveals that knowing-that and knowing-how—which Ryle argued were distinct but which much subsequent epistemology has treated as closely linked—come apart systematically in artificial agents. LLMs can exhibit one without the other, and coherence masks which one they possess. This finding does not resolve the Ryle debate, but it provides an unexpected empirical context for it: artificial systems that dissociate what human cognition typically integrates.

6.5 Anticipated Objections

Three objections merit direct response.

1. “Is this merely a reformulation of the symbol grounding problem?” Harnad (1990) argued that symbolic systems manipulate meaningless tokens lacking sensorimotor grounding. The Coherence Paradox is related but structurally distinct. The symbol grounding problem is unidirectional: symbols fail to connect to the world. The bidirectional paradox reveals that grounding and competence can come apart in both directions. Type B—grounded without success—has no analog in the classical symbol grounding debate. A system that tracks causal structure yet fails to act effectively is not merely ungrounded; it is grounded but impotent. This second failure mode requires new conceptual tools beyond the grounding framework.

2. “Two domains cannot establish a general pattern.” This is correct: two domains establish possibility, not prevalence. But establishing possibility suffices for the philosophical argument. The widespread assumption that coherence reliably signals grounding is a universal claim—it asserts that coherent explanations are trustworthy regardless of domain. A single counterexample refutes a universal claim; two counterexamples exhibiting opposite patterns refute it decisively. What remains open is how common the inversion is across domains, which is an empirical question for future work. The conceptual contribution—that coherence can mask opposite epistemic failures depending on conditions—stands independently of prevalence.

3. “Future architectures may resolve the dissociation.” This is possible and would be welcome. But the philosophical analysis does not depend on the dissociation being permanent. The integrated justification framework identifies what would need to be true for genuine understanding to be attributed: coherence, grounding, and proper basing. If future architectures achieve this integration, the framework provides the criteria for recognizing the achievement. If they do not, it explains why. Either way, the framework is diagnostic, not pessimistic.

7 Conclusion

I have introduced the Bidirectional Coherence Paradox—the phenomenon whereby the relationship between explanatory coherence and empirical grounding not only dissociates but inverts across epistemic conditions. The 61-percentage-point swing observed between the low-observability compiler domain (+31pp gap favoring action over explanation) and the high-observability HPO domain (–30pp gap favoring explanation over action) demonstrates that coherence and grounding can be systematically opposed, not merely independent—at least under the conditions studied here.

This bidirectional pattern has significant implications:

  • •

    For epistemology: Neither coherentism, foundationalism, nor Haack’s foundherentism alone captures the epistemology of artificial reasoning. Adequate evaluation requires a tripartite structure—coherence, grounding, and a proper basing relation—that I term integrated justification.

  • •

    For AI evaluation: AI systems cannot be assessed by coherence alone (Type A shows this misleads) nor by grounding alone (Type B shows this is insufficient). What is needed are metrics that capture the basing relation—whether correct actions flow from correct understanding, not merely accompany it.

  • •

    For trust: The Type A Paradox reveals that AI successes may be epistemically lucky—correct outcomes achieved through mechanisms the system does not understand. Trust should be calibrated to the observability regime: in low-observability domains, even successful AI explanations may be confabulations.

  • •

    For the knowing-that/knowing-how debate: Ryle’s distinction receives unexpected empirical illustration. LLMs exhibit knowing-how without knowing-that (Type A) and knowing-that without knowing-how (Type B)—dissociating what human cognition typically integrates. These are different failure modes, not degrees of the same capacity.

The Epistemic Triangle model explains this bidirectional pattern: observability determines whether prior-dominated or signal-dominated reasoning prevails, producing qualitatively different failure modes.

Further implications. The findings raise additional concerns that merit future investigation. First, LLM explanations may constitute a novel form of pseudo-testimony—outputs that resemble testimony without the underlying belief states that normally justify testimonial acceptance. Second, the combination of high coherence and low grounding creates persuasive confabulators: systems that become more convincing precisely when they are less reliable. Third, these findings have implications for Chain-of-Thought prompting: coherent reasoning chains may improve performance while misrepresenting the actual basis for success—the chain functions as scaffolding for pattern retrieval rather than a trace of genuine inference.

Fourth, and most directly connected to the basing relation analysis, subsidiary experiments reveal that LLMs function as one-shot reasoners, degrading rather than improving with extended feedback (Appendix B). This reinforces the absence of proper basing: if outputs were genuinely based on accumulated evidence, performance should improve with additional feedback. Instead, extended context introduces noise. Each response is generated from immediate priors rather than refined through iterative grounding. The system does not learn from feedback in any epistemically meaningful sense—it retrieves patterns anew each time.

The path forward may require not merely better models, but architectural transformations coupled with a more adequate epistemology—frameworks for understanding what AI systems can and cannot know, given their epistemic situation. Perhaps the deepest lesson is humility: understanding and competence can come apart in ways that challenge our intuitions about mind, knowledge, and agency. If these dissociations are stable features of current AI architectures, new conceptual tools must be developed for navigating a world where artificial systems may be coherent without being grounded, or grounded without being competent.

The bidirectional paradox documented here exemplifies what such tools might reveal. We do not learn about AI when it succeeds—we learn when it succeeds for the wrong reasons, or fails for the right ones.

Appendix A Detailed Methodology

This appendix provides technical details for the empirical methodology summarized in Section 3.

A.1 Metric-Reasoning Loop (MRL) Framework

The Metric-Reasoning Loop (MRL) is not designed as a state-of-the-art optimization system, but as an epistemic probe: a controlled environment for exposing the relationship between explanatory coherence and empirical grounding in LLM reasoning. Its purpose is diagnostic, not competitive. Figure 5 shows the MRL pipeline as applied to the first domain, the compiler optimization domain.

The experiments employed a closed-loop optimization framework where an LLM iteratively: (1) observes system metrics, (2) generates an abductive hypothesis about the bottleneck, (3) selects an intervention, and (4) receives feedback on the outcome. The LLM was constrained to produce structured JSON outputs with explicit reasoning chains, enabling separate assessment of coherence and grounding.

To minimize experimental noise, all experiments were executed serially within the framework, avoiding parallel processes that could compete for resources or introduce measurement overhead in observability.

A.2 Compiler Optimization Domain

Testbed. PolyBench/C 4.2 benchmarks compiled with Clang 15 at -O2 optimization level. Ten benchmarks were selected: 2mm, 3mm, atax, bicg, gemm, gemver, heat-3d, jacobi-2d, mvt, and seidel-2d.

Observable Metrics. Hardware performance counters captured via Linux perf: instructions per cycle (IPC), L1 data cache miss rate, and branch misprediction rate. These metrics are known to be noisy proxies for microarchitectural phenomena.

Action Space. 12 pragma-based interventions across 4 categories: loop unrolling (#pragma clang loop unroll), vectorization (#pragma clang loop vectorize), interleaving (#pragma clang loop interleave), and prefetching (__builtin_prefetch).

Experimental Protocol. Each benchmark was run for 10 MRL iterations with 20 repetitions per configuration for statistical stability. Total: over 4,000 controlled executions across all strategies.

A.3 Hyperparameter Optimization Domain

Testbed. A simple CNN (∼\sim530K parameters) trained on CIFAR-10. The model architecture: 3 convolutional layers with batch normalization, followed by 2 fully connected layers.

Observable Metrics. Direct access to: training loss, validation loss, validation accuracy, gradient norm (mean and max), loss variance across batches, and convergence rate (moving average of loss improvement).

Action Space. 24 hyperparameter interventions across 5 categories: learning rate modifications (increase/decrease by factors of 2×\times, 5×\times; cosine/warmup schedules), batch size modifications, regularization (dropout, weight decay), optimizer changes (Adam, SGD, AdamW), and gradient control (clipping enable/disable).

Experimental Protocol. 10 MRL iterations with 10 training epochs per trial. Baseline accuracy: 78.6%; best achieved: 82.4%.

A.4 Extended Discussion of ASR Limitations

The ASR metric warrants extended discussion beyond the summary in the main text.

False positives occur when the hypothesized metric changes in the predicted direction for reasons unrelated to the stated mechanism. In complex systems with correlated variables, a metric may improve coincidentally with an intervention. The intervention need not cause the improvement through the hypothesized pathway.

False negatives occur when the stated mechanism is correct but the target metric does not change observably. This can happen when effects are delayed, when measurement noise obscures real changes, or when the correct mechanism operates at a level of granularity finer than our metrics capture.

Metric selection effects introduce systematic bias. The choice of which metrics to monitor partly determines which hypotheses can be validated. Mechanisms operating through unmeasured channels will systematically receive lower ASR scores regardless of their validity.

More broadly, any metric of grounding in artificial systems will necessarily be proxy-relative. In complex systems we typically lack direct access to the complete causal structure; therefore we evaluate a weaker, operational target: whether explanations yield correct interventional predictions about the observables we can measure. This is not a defect of the present methodology but a general feature of epistemic evaluation in opaque systems—and, arguably, in scientific practice more broadly.

Superficial grounding and its implications. ASR captures functional, intervention-oriented grounding—whether stated hypotheses correctly anticipate metric changes under the specified intervention—which is weaker than establishing a full symbol–world grounding or uniquely identifying the true causal mechanism. An explanation can track metric changes without grasping why the mechanism operates. “SGD causes instability” may correlate with gradient variance increases without understanding the loss landscape dynamics. But for black-box systems, functional grounding is the only grounding we can assess. This is the same standard applied to scientific models: a climate model is grounded not because we directly observe atmospheric dynamics at all scales, but because its predictions track outcomes. The paradox operates at the level of superficial tracking, which is precisely the level at which current AI evaluation practices operate. This is as much a critique of our epistemic practices as of the systems we evaluate.

A.5 Extended Discussion of Alternative Explanations

Several non-observability factors deserve detailed consideration beyond the summary in the main text.

Action space structure. The compiler domain has a smaller, more constrained action space (12 pragmas) than the HPO domain (24 hyperparameter modifications). Constrained spaces may favor action success by limiting poor choices; larger spaces may favor explanation accuracy by providing more degrees of freedom for diagnosis. However, action space size alone cannot explain the inversion. If larger spaces simply made both metrics worse, one would see uniform degradation—not the selective improvement in ASR coupled with degradation in ActSR observed here.

Temperature and sampling. Experiments used temperature 0 for deterministic outputs. This eliminates sampling variance but may systematically affect the action-explanation relationship by favoring modal (most-likely) responses. Preliminary tests at temperature 0.3 showed similar qualitative patterns, though a systematic study of temperature effects remains for future work.

Autoregressive generation. LLMs generate explanations token-by-token, with each token conditioned on previous tokens. This sequential structure optimizes for local coherence, which may favor plausible-sounding mechanisms over accurate ones. The autoregressive architecture may be a confound rather than the observability difference per se. However, this explanation struggles to account for why high observability improves explanation accuracy.

Prior strength asymmetry. The compiler domain has stronger, more consistent priors in training data (decades of optimization folklore) than the HPO domain (heterogeneous practices, rapid methodological change). This asymmetry might explain why compiler actions succeed despite poor explanations: transferred heuristics are more reliable. Weaker HPO priors may explain why explanations must rely more on observable signals.

Domain complexity. Hyperparameter interactions are notoriously complex and context-dependent; compiler optimizations on simple loop nests are comparatively predictable. Higher domain complexity in HPO might impair action selection independently of observability.

A.6 LLM Configuration

Primary model: Claude Opus 4.5 (claude-opus-4-5-20251101) at temperature 0 for deterministic outputs. Validation: GPT-5.2 with equivalent settings. Both models received identical system prompts enforcing structured JSON output with explicit abductive reasoning. All experiments were conducted between late December 2025 and late January 2026.

Appendix B Ablation Studies

B.1 Context Window Size

An ablation study over history window size (K∈{3,5,10}K\in\{3,5,10\}) revealed counterintuitive dynamics. Mean ActSR peaked at K=5K=5 (33.3%) and declined at K=10K=10 (20.0%), with high variance across benchmarks: heat-3d dropped from 50% to 0% ActSR when moving from K=5K=5 to K=10K=10, while gemm showed the opposite pattern (0% at K=5K=5, 40% at K=10K=10).

This inconsistency suggests LLMs function as one-shot reasoners that apply immediate priors but fail to extract reliable patterns from extended feedback. Additional history may help or hurt depending on benchmark-specific interactions, but on average introduces more noise than signal.

B.2 Extended Reasoning Modes

Testing Claude Opus 4.5 Extended Thinking and GPT-5.2 High Reasoning Effort revealed that deep reasoning modes reduce paradox rate (from 50% to 20%) but do not improve optimization performance. The standard model achieved highest speedup despite highest paradox rate; extended thinking achieved lowest paradox rate but worst performance.

This suggests a trade-off between epistemic caution and explorative boldness: extended reasoning increases self-consistency while reducing willingness to act on uncertain hypotheses.
